questions.q: In the 2-qubit circuit with CNOT (control=qubit 1, target=qubit 2), why does qubit 1's own marginal probability stay exactly the same before and after the CNOT?
options: Because qubit 1 was never actually rotated by any gate in this circuit
Because the circuit was run on a classical simulator rather than real hardware
A CNOT only permutes amplitudes within the block where the control is |1>, never moving probability between the control being |0> and |1>, so the control qubit's own marginal is always unchanged
Because CNOT only works correctly when both qubits start in |0>
questions.explain: This is a general, exact property of CNOT: it swaps amplitudes only within the control=1 subspace, which can never change the total probability of the control being 0 versus 1 -- confirmed numerically in the lab (P(qubit1=0)=0.5 both before and after).

questions.q: Before the CNOT, qubit 2's marginal <Z> equals cos(pi/3) = 0.5 exactly. After the CNOT (with qubit 1 as control), what does <Z> on qubit 2 become, and what does that demonstrate?
options: 1.0, the maximum possible value
The CNOT has no well-defined effect on qubit 2's marginal
Still exactly 0.5, unchanged by the CNOT
0.0000 -- a real, computed change caused entirely by entangling qubit 2 with qubit 1, something no un-entangled single-qubit circuit could produce
questions.explain: Direct computation shows P(qubit2=0) and P(qubit2=1) both become exactly 0.5 after the CNOT, giving <Z>=0 -- a genuine, verified shift from the pre-entanglement value of 0.5, demonstrating entanglement's real effect on the target qubit.

questions.q: After layer 2's rotations and CNOT (theta3=pi/5, theta4=pi/7 added on top of layer 1), what happens to the <Z> measurements on both qubits?
options: Both <Z> on qubit 1 (approx -0.509) and qubit 2 (approx 0.619) now depend on the full set of all four parameters theta1 through theta4, not just their 'own' qubit's rotation angles
Both measurements return to exactly their single-qubit values, unaffected by the second layer
The second layer has no effect at all on either qubit's measurement
Only qubit 1's measurement changes; qubit 2's stays exactly as it was after layer 1
questions.explain: The verified computation shows both qubits' final measurements mix information from all four rotation angles after two rounds of entanglement -- neither matches any single-qubit-only calculation, demonstrating how depth increases expressiveness.

questions.q: Why does entanglement's effect show up on qubit 2 after just ONE CNOT layer, while qubit 1 only shows a genuinely 'mixed' measurement after a SECOND layer is added?
options: CNOT never changes its own control qubit's marginal (so qubit 1's single-CNOT marginal stays pure), but it does change the target qubit's marginal; only once a second rotation+CNOT layer feeds information back through qubit 1's rotation does qubit 1's own measurement start mixing in qubit 2's influence
There is no real difference; both qubits are affected identically after one layer
Because qubit 1 is physically a different type of qubit than qubit 2 in this circuit
Because qubit 2 was measured first in the circuit, giving it priority
questions.explain: This follows directly from the control-invariance property of CNOT: the target's marginal changes immediately, but the control's marginal is only affected once a further gate (the next layer's rotation, applied to the now-entangled state) acts on it.

questions.q: Why does this lab's use of only 2 qubits NOT demonstrate anything about barren plateaus, even though the lesson discusses how depth worsens that effect?
options: Barren plateaus require many qubits to show their exponential-in-qubit-count gradient-vanishing effect; 2 qubits is far too small a system to exhibit it
Barren plateaus only occur in single-qubit circuits, never multi-qubit ones
Barren plateaus are unrelated to qubit count entirely
This lab actually does demonstrate a real barren plateau in its layer-2 results
questions.explain: The lab explicitly notes this limitation: barren plateaus are specifically an exponential-in-qubit-count phenomenon, so a 2-qubit toy circuit is far too small to exhibit it -- its only purpose here is making entanglement mechanics concrete and checkable by hand.
